result.brief:
# Brief: "Cores" lecture slides (Processamento de Imagens, Prof. Thiago Raposo Milhomem, Centro Universitário IESB)

The PDF has no text layer, so I read all 32 slides visually. The slides are in Portuguese. Most figures are from Gonzalez & Woods (Figs. 6.1–6.10, Table 6.1). The slides contain **no worked numeric exercises and no algorithms**. They are conceptual, with a few formulas and one numeric reading of the chromaticity diagram (p. 20).

## Prerequisites referenced
- No specific earlier lecture is cited. Slide 2 says that color-image algorithms are "in general the same ideas as for monochrome images, with adaptations in some situations" (p. 2). This assumes prior knowledge of grayscale/monochrome processing.
- Basic electromagnetic spectrum and wavelength (nm) are assumed (pp. 3–4).

## 1. Introduction (pp. 1–2)
- p. 1 is the title slide, "Cores".
- p. 2 covers pseudo-colors, for example originally achromatic images that are colorized.
- It states that the human visual system (SVH) is sensitive to only a specific part of the electromagnetic spectrum.
- Color-specific techniques listed: color coding, tonal correction and color enhancement (p. 2).

## 2. Visible spectrum (pp. 3–4)
- p. 3 (Fig. 6.2) is a diagram of the full EM spectrum: gamma rays, X-rays, UV, visible, infrared, microwaves, TV and radio. The visible band is expanded to about 400–700 nm, with UV below it and IR above it. The scale runs from 300 to 1500 nm.
- p. 4 (Fig. 6.1) shows white light through an optical prism. It splits into a rainbow, with infrared at the red end and ultraviolet at the violet end.

## 3. Human visual system (SVH) (pp. 5–9)
- p. 5 shows an eye anatomy diagram. Labeled parts: cornea, iris, anterior chamber, lens, ciliary body, ciliary muscle and fibers, vitreous humor, retina, fovea, blind spot, optic nerve, visual axis, sclera and choroid.
- p. 5 also has a plot of rods and cones per mm² against angle from the fovea (80° to 0° to 80°). Cones peak sharply at the fovea (0°). Rods peak around ±20° and drop to zero at the blind spot.
- p. 6 shows the retina cross-section and normalized spectral response curves for S, M and L cones. The peaks are roughly S≈445 nm, M≈545 nm and L≈575 nm.
- Cones (S, M, L), about 5 million (p. 6):
  - They work at "normal" light levels.
  - They allow the perception of color/light.
  - They are located at the center of the retina and give image detail.
- Rods, about 100 million (p. 6):
  - They are in the periphery.
  - They work at low light levels.
- p. 7 shows micrographs of the cone mosaic. (A) is the fovea, with densely packed cones. (B) is the periphery, with larger cones and rods filling the gaps. (C) plots cone density (×1000/mm²) against eccentricity (0–0.5 mm). Density falls with distance from the fovea (Curcio et al., 1990). It also shows a simulated red/green/blue cone mosaic.
- p. 8 is the "Eye Color Sensitivity" curve, in % sensitivity from about 400 to 700 nm. It peaks (100%) in the green region, around 550 nm, and falls toward violet and red.
- p. 9 ("Filtro em mosaico") is an isometric diagram of a Bayer-type color filter array over a sensor. Green filters appear twice as often as red or blue, in a checkerboard layout. It is the camera analogue of the cone mosaic.

## 4. Perception concepts (pp. 10–16)
- Object color (p. 10):
  - It is the absorbed versus reflected part of the spectrum, and it is a property of the body.
  - Example: green bodies reflect only the 500–570 nm band.
  - Achromatic light has no hue and minimum saturation. Its only variable attribute is intensity, and it gives a gray scale.
- Chromatic light has three measures (p. 11):
  - **Radiance** is the total energy emitted by the light source.
  - **Luminance** is the portion of that energy the observer perceives, measured in lumens (lm).
  - **Brightness** is a subjective descriptor related to luminous intensity.
- p. 12 gives the percentage of cones by color: Blue 2%, Green 33%, Red 65%. The slide titles it "Cones e Bastonetes".
- Primary colors are RGB (p. 12). CIE (Commission Internationale de l'Éclairage) standard primaries are Blue 435.8 nm, Green 546.1 nm and Red 700.0 nm (p. 12).
- p. 13 (Fig. 6.3) shows the absorption curves of the blue, green and red cones against wavelength. Peaks are at 445 nm (blue), 535 nm (green) and 575 nm (red). The wavelength axis is labeled with color names: bluish purple, purplish blue, blue, blue-green, green, yellowish green, yellow, orange, reddish orange and red.
- p. 14 (Fig. 6.4) shows primary and secondary colors, as two Venn-style diagrams:
  - Additive light: R, G and B primaries. R+G = yellow, G+B = cyan, R+B = magenta, and all three = white.
  - Subtractive pigments: yellow, magenta and cyan primaries. Yellow+magenta = red, yellow+cyan = green, magenta+cyan = blue, and all three = black.
- The color descriptors (p. 15) are:
  - **Brilho** (brightness) is the chromatic perception of intensity.
  - **Tonalidade** (hue) is the dominant wavelength where the energy is concentrated, i.e. the predominant perceived color.
  - **Saturação** is the purity of the light. Purer colors are more saturated. It is the amount of white/gray mixed into the color, so higher saturation means less mixing.
  - **Cromaticidade** (chromaticity) is the perception of saturation plus hue.

## 5. Tristimulus values and the CIE chromaticity diagram (pp. 16–23)
- Tristimulus coefficients (p. 16):
  $$x=\frac{X}{X+Y+Z},\quad y=\frac{Y}{X+Y+Z},\quad z=\frac{Z}{X+Y+Z},\quad x+y+z=1$$
- p. 17: CIE defines 3 primaries X, Y, Z (1931). The slide gives:
  $$X=\int E(\lambda)\,\bar{x}(\lambda)\,d\lambda,\quad Y=\int E(\lambda)\,\bar{y}(\lambda)\,d\lambda,\quad Z=\int E(\lambda)\,\bar{z}(\lambda)\,d\lambda$$
  - The slide plots the color-matching functions $\bar x(\lambda)$, $\bar y(\lambda)$ and $\bar z(\lambda)$ over 400–700 nm. $\bar z$ peaks at about 1.8 near 445 nm. $\bar y$ peaks at about 1.0 near 555 nm. $\bar x$ has a small bump of about 0.35 near 445 nm and a main peak of about 1.05 near 600 nm.
  - It also shows a 3D X-Y-Z cone of colors whose projection gives the 2D chromaticity diagram, and a CIE Lab-style cylinder. That cylinder has L=100 white at the top and black at the bottom, +a red, −a green, +b yellow and −b blue.
- p. 18 shows the chromaticity diagram (x horizontal, y vertical) with the horseshoe boundary labeled in nm (380–700). An inscribed RGB triangle contains the D65 white point near (0.31, 0.33). Photos on the same slide illustrate additive mixing (colored lights on a brick wall) and subtractive mixing (paint).
- p. 19 is the annotated CIE diagram. The curved boundary is the "spectral energy locus" (wavelength in nm). Labeled regions and points: green, gold, warm white, cool white, daylight, pink, red, deep blue and blue. The "point of equal energy" is near (0.33, 0.33).
- **Worked reading (p. 20):** the point marked "Green" on the diagram has 25% red, 62% green and 13% blue.
  - The x-axis is red, so x≈0.25. The y-axis is green, so y≈0.62.
  - The blue amount comes from z = 1 − (x + y) = 1 − 0.87 = 0.13.
- p. 21: the boundary of the diagram is maximum saturation. The limits of the visible spectrum (SVH) are circled at the two ends, near 380 nm (violet/blue) and about 700–780 nm (red).
- p. 22 gives two more annotations:
  - The equi-energy point has all colors in the same proportion, saturation equal to zero, and gray intensities (white = maximum gray).
  - A "reta de cores" (color line) is the set of all colors obtainable by combining two colors.
- p. 23 (Fig. 6.6) shows the gamut ("capacidade") of real devices on the diagram. A triangle with vertices R, G and B is the typical gamut of color monitors. A smaller irregular region is the gamut of color printers. Neither covers the whole horseshoe.

## 6. Color spaces (representations) (pp. 24–32)
- p. 24 lists the main spaces:
  - **RGB** is used in monitors, cameras and projectors.
  - **CMY** (cyan, magenta, yellow) is rarely used in this form.
  - **CMYK** (adds black, K) is used by printers in general.
  - **HSI** (hue, saturation, intensity) is a synonym of HSV (hue, saturation, value). It is a perceptual model. Intensity is separated from chromaticity, so intensity can be used on its own by "black-and-white" devices that don't use chromaticity.
- p. 25 shows the RGB cube in 8-bit Cartesian coordinates:
  - Black is [0,0,0] and white is [255,255,255].
  - Pure red is [255,0,0], green [0,255,0] and blue [0,0,255].
  - Cyan is [0,255,255], magenta [255,0,255] and yellow [255,255,0].
  - The diagonal from black to white is the gray axis, where R=G=B.
  - The secondaries are sums of pairs of primaries: magenta = R+B, yellow = R+G, cyan = G+B.
  - Its axis orientation differs slightly from p. 26.
- p. 26 compares RGB (Cartesian) with HSV (cylindrical). The value/intensity axis runs along the gray diagonal. The radial distance from the gray axis is saturation. The azimuth angle around the gray axis is the hue angle. The figure's axes are labeled differently from p. 25: here Blue is vertical and Green is along the depth axis.
- p. 27 (Fig. 6.7) is a normalized RGB cube with coordinates in [0,1]. Black is at the origin, white at (1,1,1), red at (1,0,0), green at (0,1,0) and blue at (0,0,1). Cyan, magenta and yellow are at the remaining corners, and the gray scale lies on the main diagonal.
- p. 28 (Fig. 6.8) covers RGB full color: 24 bits, with (2⁸)³ = 16,777,216 colors. It shows the color cube image.
- p. 29 (Fig. 6.9) shows how an RGB image is generated from three 8-bit component planes (R, G, B) fed into a color monitor. The example is the cross-sectional plane (127, G, B). Three small images show the hidden faces of the cube at R=0, G=0 and B=0.
- Safe colors (pp. 30–32):
  - p. 30 (Table 6.1) says each RGB component of a safe color takes one of six values: hex 00, 33, 66, 99, CC, FF, which are decimal 0, 51, 102, 153, 204, 255.
  - By implication, 6³ = 216 safe colors. The slide's caption says "the 216 safe RGB colors" (Fig. 6.10a).
  - Fig. 6.10b shows the 256 grays of RGB (000000 through FFFFFF). The grays that are safe are underlined: 00, 33, 66, 99, CC and FF.
  - p. 31 shows the safe-color cube as a 6×6×6 lattice of discrete blocks.
  - p. 32 compares the continuous full-color cube (left) with the discrete safe-color cube (right).
